auraIntro: Explorer, Cartwheel Galaxy was reshaped by a violent head-on galactic collision, creating expanding shockwaves of star formation.
overview: The Cartwheel Galaxy (ESO 350-40) is a famous ring galaxy located approximately 500 million light-years away in the constellation Sculptor.
formation: Formed roughly 500 million years ago when a small companion galaxy punched directly through the center of a larger spiral galaxy.
structure: A ring galaxy spanning 150,000 light-years across. It features an inner ring surrounding the core and an outer ring expanding at 217,000 mph.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in 1941 by Fritz Zwicky, who described it as 'one of the most complicated structures waiting for an explanation.'
observationTips: Extremely distant at 500 million light-years; imaged extensively by Hubble and JWST's NIRCam and MIRI instruments.
funFacts: Created when a smaller companion galaxy pierced straight through the center of a spiral galaxy like a pebble dropped in a pond.
The outer ring is expanding at over 217,000 mph (350,000 km/h), plowing into surrounding gas and sparking starbursts.

cards.title: Arrival: The Wheel of Fire
cards.subtitle: ESO 350-40 Overview
cards.body: Welcome to the Cartwheel Galaxy (ESO 350-40), one of the most remarkable collision ring galaxies in the observable universe. Located 500 million light-years away in the constellation Sculptor, Cartwheel spans 150,000 light-years across space. Its dramatic wagon-wheel shape was created by a violent, high-speed cosmic crash.

cards.title: Discovery: Fritz Zwicky's Enigma
cards.subtitle: 1941 Discovery to Space Telescopes
cards.body: Discovered in 1941 by Swiss astrophysicist Fritz Zwicky at Palomar Observatory, Zwicky called Cartwheel 'one of the most complicated structures waiting for an explanation'. Decades later, supercomputer simulations confirmed Zwicky's hypothesis that Cartwheel was produced by a bullseye collision.
bulletPoints: Fritz Zwicky first cataloged Cartwheel at Palomar Observatory in 1941.
Initial theories debated whether it was a single galaxy or colliding pair.
Confirmed as a head-on collision ring galaxy by computer hydrodynamic modeling.

cards.title: Cosmic Story: Shockwaves Like a Pebble in a Pond
cards.subtitle: 217,000 mph Expanding Density Wave
cards.body: Approximately 500 million years ago, a smaller companion galaxy plunged directly through the center of Cartwheel's parent spiral disk. Like a pebble dropped into a quiet pond, the impact sent a high-speed gravitational shockwave expanding outward at over 217,000 mph (350,000 km/h), sweeping up gas and igniting a ring of massive star formation.
bulletPoints: Gravitational shockwave expands outward at 217,000 mph.
Sweeps up interstellar gas, igniting intense starbursts in the outer ring.
Outer ring is rich in massive, short-lived supernova progenitor stars.

cards.title: Deep Insight: Webb NIRCam & MIRI Composite
cards.subtitle: Unveiling Dusty Spokes in Mid-Infrared
cards.body: NASA's James Webb Space Telescope imaged Cartwheel with NIRCam (Near-Infrared Camera) and MIRI (Mid-Infrared Instrument). Webb revealed faint optical 'spokes' connecting the inner bright core to the expanding outer ring, showing silicate dust filaments and young star clusters that optical telescopes could not see.
bulletPoints: JWST NIRCam & MIRI combined view reveals glowing dust spokes.
Dust spokes consist mainly of silicate dust and complex hydrocarbon molecules.
Outer ring glows in mid-infrared wavelengths due to hot starburst dust.

cards.title: Cosmic Curiosity: Transient Evolutionary Phase
cards.subtitle: Reconstructing a Spiral Galaxy
cards.body: Cartwheel is caught in a transient, temporary stage of galaxy evolution. Over the next several hundred million years, as the outer expansion ring dissipates, gravity will pull material back together, and Cartwheel will gradually rebuild its traditional spiral arms.
bulletPoints: Ring structure is temporary, lasting a few hundred million years.
Gravity will eventually reshape Cartwheel into a normal spiral galaxy.
Serves as a rare laboratory for studying galaxy resilience and shockwave physics.
